newsitem.title: USA: End not near for Miami tobacco trial.
newsitem.headline: End not near for Miami tobacco trial.

text.p: As a landmark Miami secondhand smoke trial ended its second month last week, one participant likened the long case to the journey undertaken 478 years ago by the Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan, who began the first trip around the world.

When Magellan left Seville in 1519, he was not sure where he was going and had no idea how long it would take him, but he knew he was going a long way as he left on what would be a three-year mission, one that immortalised him but cost him his life.
By Sunday, the Miami case, Norma Broin et al versus Philip Morris Cos Inc et al, was seeming a similar undertaking.

The suit was filed in 1991. Jury selection began on June 2, six years later, only after months of pre-trial hearings that themselves followed the tobacco industry's long fight to keep the case from being certified as a class action.

The day jury selection began, Norma Broin, the non-smoking flight attendant whose bout with lung cancer led her to pursue the case, said she was "ecstatic" to have come so far. "It's been six long years, working up to this point."
But Broin's trial was only beginning.

In the case, a class of Broin and thousands of other non- smoking flight attendants is suing the tobacco industry over lung cancer and other illnesses they blame on breathing secondhand cigarette smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets.
It is the first secondhand smoke and first class action suit against big tobacco to make it to trial.
Opening arguments began July 14, after six weeks of jury selection, with the first plaintiffs' witnesses called to the stand two days later.

Testimony also has moved slowly. The plaintiffs attorneys, Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt, and attorneys for the 10 tobacco defendants, each submitted lists of about 40 witnesses, who would appear live and in taped depositions.
All 80 of the doctors, psychiatrists, industry executives, airline pilots and others whose names appear on the witness lists are not expected to testify.
But after three weeks of witnesses, the Rosenblatts had worked their way through only about half the names on their list.
Susan Rosenblatt attributed the slow pace to the tobacco industry attorneys' frequent objections, and what she said was their desire to prolong the case as long as possible.

"We don't have a lot of control over these things," she said. "Our preference would be that it would go faster, but the tobacco industry objects constantly, and each time they object it delays things."
Tobacco attorneys, who decline comment to reporters about particulars in the case, have previously denied any intentions to prolong the proceedings.
Jurors are barred from talking to reporters, but the panel of 13 -- six jurors and seven alternates -- has shown signs of weariness with the long, often technical testimony.

This week, jurors stifled yawns, leaned on their arms, rocked back and forth, and otherwise struggled to stay alert during four hours watching a videotaped deposition taken from an 81-year-old Swiss-born pathologist.

Speaking in heavily accented English, the pathologist was questioned at length about his decision to use the word "cancer" rather than the 14-syllable medical term "pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia" in a 1973 report on the effect of smoke inhalation on hamsters.
Even Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye leaned back behind the bench, took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes as the taped medical testimony went on.
Industry analysts have said the giant case could collapse under its own weight if it goes on long enough.

In the two-stage trial, the jury will have to decide on damages for the plaintiffs after completion of the long testimony on whether secondhand smoke causes illnesses and whether tobacco companies are liable.
And participants, some of whom refused to be quoted by name, would only shrug their shoulders or shudder, at the thought of an appeal. UST.N LTR.N BGL.N
